title: Narrative Technique
subtitle: Master point of view, pacing and the art of the ending

lessons.title: Le point de vue
lessons.description: Distinguish internal, external and omniscient focalisation, and learn how French marks whose eyes a story is told through.

blocks.heading: La focalisation interne
blocks.body: In internal focalisation, the narration stays locked inside one character's head: we see, hear and understand only what that character perceives, no more. French marks this restriction through verbs of perception (apercevoir, sentir, deviner) and through gaps the narrator refuses to fill.

examples.french: Elle entendit un bruit dans le couloir, sans savoir s'il venait de l'intérieur ou du dehors.
examples.english: She heard a noise in the corridor, without knowing whether it came from inside or outside.
examples.note: the narrator knows no more than the character at this instant

examples.french: Marc crut reconnaître une silhouette, mais la pluie brouillait tout.
examples.english: Marc thought he recognised a silhouette, but the rain blurred everything.
examples.note: "crut" (from croire) signals a perception the text never confirms

examples.french: Pourquoi cette lettre était-elle restée fermée ? Elle n'osait pas se le demander.
examples.english: Why had that letter stayed unopened? She did not dare ask herself.
examples.note: the free indirect question keeps us inside her hesitation

blocks.tip: Watch for verbs like sembler, croire, deviner, avoir l'impression que — they are the grammatical fingerprints of internal focalisation.

blocks.heading: La focalisation externe
blocks.body: External focalisation keeps the camera outside every character: the narrator reports actions, words and appearances like a witness, but never enters a mind. Feelings can only be inferred from behaviour, never stated directly — this is the technique behind hard-boiled and behaviourist fiction.

examples.french: L'homme s'arrêta devant la vitrine, alluma une cigarette, puis repartit sans se retourner.
examples.english: The man stopped in front of the shop window, lit a cigarette, then walked off without looking back.
examples.note: pure external observation — no access to what he thinks or feels

examples.french: Elle ne répondit rien. Ses mains tremblaient légèrement sur la table.
examples.english: She said nothing. Her hands trembled slightly on the table.
examples.note: emotion is shown through a visible detail, never named

examples.french: Le juge referma le dossier et regarda longuement par la fenêtre.
examples.english: The judge closed the file and looked out of the window for a long time.
examples.note: the reader must guess the judge's thoughts from the gesture alone

blocks.tip: If a sentence could be filmed exactly as written, with no voice-over of inner thought, it is almost certainly externally focalised.

blocks.heading: La focalisation zéro (le narrateur omniscient)
blocks.body: Zero focalisation — the omniscient narrator — knows everything: every character's thoughts, the past and the future, events happening in different places at once. French signals this with sweeping generalisations, simultaneous scenes joined by pendant ce temps, and direct commentary on characters the characters themselves cannot make.

examples.french: Pendant que Julien dormait, sa sœur, à trois cents kilomètres de là, préparait déjà sa réponse.
examples.english: While Julien slept, his sister, three hundred kilometres away, was already preparing her answer.
examples.note: the narrator moves freely between two simultaneous scenes

examples.french: Il ignorait encore que cette décision allait ruiner sa carrière.
examples.english: He did not yet know that this decision would ruin his career.
examples.note: the narrator knows the future the character cannot see

examples.french: Les deux hommes se méfiaient l'un de l'autre, chacun pour des raisons que l'autre ignorait.
examples.english: The two men distrusted each other, each for reasons the other did not know.
examples.note: the narrator enters both consciousnesses at once

blocks.tip: Omniscience is rarely announced — spot it by the narrator crossing a boundary no single character could cross: time, distance, or another mind.

blocks.heading: Le discours indirect libre
blocks.body: Free indirect style blends the narrator's voice with a character's thoughts, without a reporting verb ("il pensa que") or quotation marks. The tense stays that of narration (imparfait, conditionnel) but the vocabulary, rhythm and exclamations belong to the character — this is the grammatical engine of internal focalisation.

examples.french: Il regarda l'heure. Encore deux heures à attendre !
examples.english: He looked at the time. Two more hours to wait!
examples.note: the exclamation is his, though no verb of thought introduces it

examples.french: Elle referma la porte. Jamais elle n'accepterait une chose pareille.
examples.english: She closed the door. Never would she accept such a thing.
examples.note: conditional-style resolve voiced through the narrator's imparfait/plus-que-parfait system

examples.french: Comparez : « Il pensa qu'il devait partir » (discours indirect) et « Il devait partir » (discours indirect libre).
examples.english: Compare: "He thought he had to leave" (indirect speech) and "He had to leave" (free indirect style).
examples.note: removing "il pensa que" fuses narrator and character

blocks.tip: If you can silently insert "il pensa que" or "elle se disait que" before a sentence without changing its tense, you are likely reading free indirect style.

blocks.heading: Les verbes de perception et de savoir
blocks.body: Verbs like sembler, paraître, croire, deviner, ignorer que, avoir l'impression que grammatically mark the limits of a character's knowledge — the narrator refuses to confirm what only seems true. With ignorer que and douter que, the subjunctive can appear when the doubt is genuine, sharpening the sense of restricted access.

examples.french: Il semblait avoir déjà tout compris, mais rien ne le confirmait.
examples.english: He seemed to have already understood everything, but nothing confirmed it.
examples.note: "semblait" keeps the truth outside the narrator's authority

examples.french: Elle doutait qu'il fût vraiment parti.
examples.english: She doubted that he had really left.
examples.note: subjunctive after douter que signals genuine uncertainty inside her mind

examples.french: Il ignorait que sa sœur, à ce moment précis, prenait le train.
examples.english: He did not know that his sister, at that very moment, was taking the train.
examples.note: ignorer que + indicative: the fact is true, only the character is blind to it

blocks.tip: Distinguish croire/sembler (the character's uncertain belief) from ignorer que + indicative (a true fact the character simply does not know) — the second is the classic marker of dramatic irony under omniscience.

items.french: Le narrateur ignorait encore que sa décision allait tout changer.
options: The narrator already knew everything would change.

The narrator refused to make a decision.
The narrator changed his mind at the last second.
items.answer: The narrator did not yet know his decision would change everything.

passages.title: La Valise (nouvelle inédite d'Aline Rocher)
passages.french:
Elle posa la valise sur le lit sans savoir pourquoi ses mains tremblaient autant.
Le train partait dans quarante minutes, et pourtant elle n'arrivait pas à choisir quoi emporter.
Un bruit, en bas, la fit sursauter : quelqu'un montait l'escalier, lentement, comme s'il hésitait à chaque marche.
Elle retint son souffle, persuadée qu'il s'agissait de son frère venu la convaincre de rester.
Les pas s'arrêtèrent derrière la porte. Un long silence suivit, plus inquiétant qu'aucun mot n'aurait pu l'être.
Peut-être n'était-ce qu'un voisin, se dit-elle, sans y croire vraiment.
Elle referma la valise d'un geste sec, comme pour se donner une contenance.
La poignée de la porte tourna avec une lenteur presque théâtrale.
Elle ne voyait, dans l'entrebâillement, qu'une ombre qu'elle ne parvenait pas à identifier.
« C'est toi ? » demanda-t-elle, la voix mal assurée.
Aucune réponse ne vint, seulement un léger raclement, comme celui d'un vêtement contre le mur.
Elle songea, l'espace d'un instant, à toutes les personnes que cette silhouette aurait pu être.
Le train, elle le savait, n'attendrait pas.
Elle empoigna la valise et avança vers la porte, le cœur battant plus vite que ses pas.
Ce qui se trouvait réellement derrière cette porte, ni elle ni le lecteur ne le sauraient avant la page suivante.
Elle tendit la main vers la poignée, et le récit, à cet instant précis, se tut.
passages.english:
She put the suitcase on the bed without knowing why her hands were trembling so much.
The train left in forty minutes, and yet she could not manage to choose what to take.
A noise, downstairs, made her jump: someone was climbing the stairs, slowly, as if hesitating on every step.
She held her breath, convinced it was her brother come to persuade her to stay.
The footsteps stopped behind the door. A long silence followed, more unsettling than any word could have been.
Maybe it was only a neighbour, she told herself, without really believing it.
She snapped the suitcase shut, as if to give herself composure.
The door handle turned with an almost theatrical slowness.
Through the gap she could see only a shadow she could not identify.
"Is that you?" she asked, her voice unsteady.
No answer came, only a faint scraping sound, like fabric brushing the wall.
For a moment she thought of everyone that silhouette could possibly be.
The train, she knew, would not wait.
She grabbed the suitcase and moved towards the door, her heart beating faster than her steps.
What was really behind that door, neither she nor the reader would know before the next page.
She reached her hand towards the handle, and the story, at that exact instant, fell silent.

lessons.title: Le rythme du récit
lessons.description: Control narrative pace through ellipsis, scene and summary, and learn the tense system that speeds up or slows down a story.

blocks.heading: La scène et le sommaire
blocks.body: A scene stretches narrated time to match (or exceed) the time it takes to read it — dialogue, gesture-by-gesture action, sensory detail. A summary compresses months or years into a sentence. Skilled writers alternate the two deliberately: scenes for what matters, summary for what merely connects.

examples.french: « Tu pars quand ? » demanda-t-il. « Demain », répondit-elle, sans lever les yeux.
examples.english: "When are you leaving?" he asked. "Tomorrow," she answered, without looking up.
examples.note: a scene: dialogue unfolds almost in real time

examples.french: Les mois suivants furent occupés à vendre la maison, à ranger les affaires, à dire au revoir.
examples.english: The following months were spent selling the house, sorting through belongings, saying goodbye.
examples.note: a summary: months compressed into one sentence

examples.french: Le dîner dura deux heures. Le narrateur n'en raconte que les cinq dernières minutes.
examples.english: Dinner lasted two hours. The narrator recounts only the last five minutes of it.
examples.note: the ratio between story-time and text-time defines scene vs. summary

blocks.tip: Ask: does this passage take about as long to read as it took to happen? If yes, it is a scene; if the text is far shorter than the events, it is a summary.

blocks.heading: L'ellipse narrative
blocks.body: An ellipse skips narrated time altogether: nothing is told about the gap, only a marker signals that time has passed. Ellipses can be explicit (a stated duration) or implicit (a mere paragraph break, a chapter change), and they are essential for cutting the story down to what matters.

examples.french: Dix ans passèrent. Rien, dans la maison, n'avait changé.
examples.english: Ten years passed. Nothing in the house had changed.
examples.note: an explicit ellipse: the duration is stated, the content is skipped entirely

examples.french:
*** 
Quand il revint, la ville avait un nouveau maire.
examples.english:
*** 
When he came back, the town had a new mayor.
examples.note: a typographic break (implicit ellipse) does the same work with no words at all

examples.french: Le lendemain matin, tout avait déjà été décidé sans elle.
examples.english: The next morning, everything had already been decided without her.
examples.note: the plus-que-parfait signals events completed during the skipped interval

blocks.tip: The plus-que-parfait right after an ellipse is a strong clue: it packs pre-completed action into the gap the narrator chose not to narrate.

blocks.heading: Accélérer et ralentir le récit
blocks.body: Pace is not fixed for a whole book: writers speed up through dense summary and short paragraphs, then slow down through elaborate description, extended dialogue and the historic present, which makes past events feel as if they are happening now, right in front of the reader.

examples.french: Il courut, tourna à gauche, sauta par-dessus le muret, disparut.
examples.english: He ran, turned left, jumped over the low wall, disappeared.
examples.note: short clauses in rapid succession accelerate the rhythm

examples.french: Elle s'assied, pose ses mains sur la table, ferme les yeux, respire une dernière fois.
examples.english: She sits down, places her hands on the table, closes her eyes, breathes one last time.
examples.note: the historic present slows the reader down inside a single, suspended instant

examples.french: Le paysage, lui, ne se pressait pas : la brume s'effilochait lentement au-dessus des toits.
examples.english: The landscape, for its part, was in no hurry: the mist slowly frayed above the rooftops.
examples.note: extended description stretches text-time far beyond story-time

blocks.tip: Count the verbs per sentence: many short verbs in a row accelerate the rhythm; one action stretched across a long sentence slows it down.

blocks.heading: Les marqueurs temporels de l'ellipse et du sommaire
blocks.body: Ellipsis and summary rely on compressed time markers: durations (des années durant, en l'espace de quelques mois), vague adverbs (peu après, bien plus tard), and the plus-que-parfait, which packs completed action into a gap the narrator has chosen not to narrate in full.

examples.french: Des années durant, elle avait cru pouvoir oublier ce jour-là.
examples.english: For years, she had believed she could forget that day.
examples.note: "des années durant" compresses a long stretch of story time into a phrase

examples.french: Peu après, tout était redevenu comme avant.
examples.english: Shortly after, everything had gone back to normal.
examples.note: "peu après" glosses over unnarrated events

examples.french: Quand elle rouvrit les yeux, la guerre avait déjà commencé.
examples.english: When she opened her eyes again, the war had already begun.
examples.note: the plus-que-parfait places an entire unnarrated development before the resumed scene

blocks.tip: Vague time adverbs (bientôt, peu après, quelque temps plus tard) are the surface signal of an ellipse — always ask what the text is choosing not to tell.

blocks.heading: L'alternance passé simple / imparfait dans le rythme
blocks.body: In literary narration, the passé simple carries the punctual, forward-moving actions of a scene, while the imparfait provides background, description and repeated or ongoing states that slow the reader down. Shifting the balance between the two tenses is itself a way of controlling pace.

examples.french: Il pleuvait depuis le matin. Elle sortit sans parapluie.
examples.english: It had been raining since morning. She went out without an umbrella.
examples.note: imparfait sets the slow backdrop, passé simple delivers the single sharp action

examples.french: La ville dormait encore. Le camion s'arrêta devant l'immeuble.
examples.english: The town was still asleep. The truck stopped in front of the building.
examples.note: same pattern: static imparfait, then one decisive passé simple verb

examples.french: Ils marchaient depuis des heures quand ils aperçurent enfin la côte.
examples.english: They had been walking for hours when they finally spotted the coast.
examples.note: a long imparfait duration is punctuated by a single passé simple event

blocks.tip: A passage heavy with imparfait and light on passé simple will always read as slower — count the ratio to predict a passage's pace before you even finish it.

passages.title: Le Café du Matin (nouvelle inédite de Thomas Delrieu)
passages.french:
Le réveil sonna à six heures précises ; Léa l'éteignit d'un geste sec et resta immobile, les yeux ouverts dans le noir.
Elle se leva, prépara le café, écouta le bruit de la cafetière, regarda par la fenêtre la rue encore déserte.
« Encore une journée », murmura-t-elle, sans savoir si elle parlait pour elle-même ou pour personne.
Les semaines suivantes filèrent sans qu'elle s'en aperçoive vraiment : le café, la boutique, les clients, les factures.
Elle avait ouvert le magasin en mars ; en septembre, elle n'avait presque plus le temps de s'asseoir.
***
Un matin d'octobre, la porte s'ouvrit sur un homme qu'elle n'avait pas revu depuis des années.
Il resta un instant sur le seuil, hésitant, puis dit simplement : « Je suis passé par hasard. »
Léa reposa la tasse qu'elle tenait, lentement, comme si un geste brusque pouvait tout briser.
« Ça fait longtemps », répondit-elle enfin, la voix plus tremblante qu'elle ne l'aurait voulu.
Ils restèrent là, tous les deux, sans bouger, pendant ce qui parut durer une éternité mais qui ne dura, en réalité, que quelques secondes.
Dehors, un bus passa, puis un autre ; la rue reprenait sa vie ordinaire, indifférente à ce qui se jouait à l'intérieur.
Personne, dans la boutique, n'aurait pu deviner que cette rencontre allait tout changer.
Léa reposa lentement sa tasse sur le comptoir et proposa, d'une voix presque égale : « Un café ? »
passages.english:
The alarm rang at exactly six o'clock; Léa switched it off sharply and stayed still, eyes open in the dark.
She got up, made coffee, listened to the sound of the coffee maker, looked out at the still-empty street.
"Another day," she murmured, not knowing whether she was speaking to herself or to no one.
The following weeks went by without her really noticing: the coffee, the shop, the customers, the bills.
She had opened the shop in March; by September, she barely had time to sit down.
***
One October morning, the door opened onto a man she had not seen in years.
He stood a moment on the threshold, hesitant, then simply said, "I was passing by."
Léa set down the cup she was holding, slowly, as if a sudden movement might break something.
"It's been a long time," she finally replied, her voice shakier than she would have liked.
They stood there, the two of them, without moving, for what felt like an eternity but in reality lasted only a few seconds.
Outside, a bus went by, then another; the street resumed its ordinary life, indifferent to what was unfolding inside.
No one in the shop could have guessed that this meeting was about to change everything.
Léa slowly set her cup down on the counter and offered, in an almost steady voice, "Coffee?"

lessons.title: La chute
lessons.description: Analyse how French stories close: twist endings, open resolutions, and the grammar that signals an ending is coming.

blocks.heading: La chute : le retournement final
blocks.body: La chute is the very last beat of a story — the sentence or paragraph the whole text has been building towards. A twist chute reverses what the reader believed to be true; it must be surprising yet, on rereading, inevitable, prepared by details planted earlier without being obvious.

examples.french: Ce n'est qu'à la dernière ligne que le lecteur comprend que le narrateur est mort depuis le début.
examples.english: Only in the last line does the reader understand that the narrator has been dead from the start.
examples.note: a classic retrospective twist: it recontextualises everything read before

examples.french: La lettre qu'elle attendait tant venait, en réalité, d'elle-même.
examples.english: The letter she had waited for so long was, in fact, from herself.
examples.note: the reversal exploits a detail the reader assumed was settled

examples.french: Le vieil homme sourit : il savait, depuis le premier jour, ce que personne d'autre ne savait.
examples.english: The old man smiled: he had known, from the very first day, what no one else knew.
examples.note: the twist redistributes knowledge retroactively between narrator and reader

blocks.tip: A good twist chute rewards a second reading — check that earlier details, reread with the ending in mind, now make perfect sense.

blocks.heading: Le dénouement : la résolution attendue
blocks.body: Unlike a twist, a dénouement resolves the central tension the way the story has led the reader to expect: conflicts are settled, questions are answered, characters reach the state their arc was moving towards. A satisfying dénouement still needs precision — vague reassurance reads as weak, not peaceful.

examples.french: Ils se turent un long moment, puis elle lui tendit la main : tout était pardonné.
examples.english: They were silent for a long moment, then she held out her hand: everything was forgiven.
examples.note: a clean dénouement, the conflict named earlier is now resolved

examples.french: Le procès s'acheva comme chacun l'avait prévu, sans surprise ni soulagement particulier.
examples.english: The trial ended as everyone had predicted, without particular surprise or relief.
examples.note: resolution does not require drama — expected outcomes can still close a story well

examples.french: Elle reprit son travail le lundi suivant, comme si rien ne s'était passé — mais tout, en elle, avait changé.
examples.english: She went back to work the following Monday, as if nothing had happened — but everything in her had changed.
examples.note: an internal resolution can coexist with an unchanged external situation

blocks.tip: Ask what question the story opened with — a strong dénouement answers exactly that question, not a different one.

blocks.heading: La fin ouverte et la fin fermée
blocks.body: A fin fermée closes every thread definitively: the reader leaves with no unanswered question. A fin ouverte deliberately withholds a final answer, leaving the reader to imagine several possible outcomes — a technique that trusts ambiguity more than certainty.

examples.french: Elle monta dans le train. On ne saura jamais si elle est revenue.
examples.english: She got on the train. We will never know whether she came back.
examples.note: a textbook fin ouverte: the last fact deliberately withheld

examples.french: Le mariage eut lieu en juin, et les deux familles ne se quittèrent plus.
examples.english: The wedding took place in June, and the two families never parted again.
examples.note: a fin fermée: every remaining thread is explicitly tied off

examples.french: La porte resta entrouverte derrière lui. Personne ne sut jamais ce qu'il était allé chercher.
examples.english: The door stayed ajar behind him. No one ever knew what he had gone to find.
examples.note: an open ending built entirely on a single unresolved detail

blocks.tip: Look for an explicit "on ne saura jamais" / "personne ne sut" — French often marks an open ending by naming, out loud, the very thing it refuses to reveal.

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel comme futur dans le passé
blocks.body: To foreshadow an ending well before it happens, French narration uses the conditionnel as a "future in the past": from a past vantage point, it announces what will later occur, letting the reader sense the ending's shadow long before the final page.

examples.french: Il ne savait pas encore qu'il ne reviendrait jamais dans cette maison.
examples.english: He did not yet know that he would never return to that house.
examples.note: the conditionnel "reviendrait" foreshadows an outcome from inside the past narration

examples.french: Elle ignorait que cette rencontre déciderait de tout le reste de sa vie.
examples.english: She did not know that this meeting would decide the whole rest of her life.
examples.note: the same structure sets up the ending's weight far in advance

examples.french: Personne, ce soir-là, n'aurait pu deviner ce que cette lettre allait provoquer.
examples.english: No one, that evening, could have guessed what that letter was about to trigger.
examples.note: the conditionnel passé signals a consequence still to come at the time of narration

blocks.tip: "Il ne savait pas encore que + conditionnel" is a near-formulaic marker of foreshadowing — treat it as a direct signpost pointing toward the chute.

blocks.heading: Les phrases nominales et la brièveté de la chute
blocks.body: Many chutes end on a nominal sentence — a phrase without a conjugated verb — or on an unusually short sentence after longer ones. This grammatical compression mimics finality: the story runs out of words at the exact moment it runs out of things left to say.

examples.french: Un silence. Puis, plus rien.
examples.english: A silence. Then, nothing more.
examples.note: two nominal/minimal sentences close the text on pure brevity

examples.french: Elle sourit. Fin.
examples.english: She smiled. The end.
examples.note: the shortest possible closing clause after a longer narrative build-up

examples.french: La porte, enfin, se referma.
examples.english: The door, at last, finally closed.
examples.note: a single short independent clause, isolated for maximum weight

blocks.tip: Compare sentence length across the last paragraph — a sudden drop in length almost always marks the chute itself, not just the sentence before it.

passages.title: Le Dernier Client (nouvelle inédite de Sophie Anctil)
passages.french:
Le magasin allait fermer dans dix minutes lorsque la clochette de la porte retentit une dernière fois.
Bernard leva les yeux sans grand enthousiasme : encore un client, à cette heure-ci.
Un homme âgé s'avança vers le comptoir, une petite boîte en bois entre les mains.
« Je voudrais que vous l'ouvriez », dit-il simplement, en posant la boîte devant Bernard.
« Elle est verrouillée depuis si longtemps que j'en ai oublié la raison. »
Bernard examina la serrure, minuscule et rouillée, avec l'œil d'un homme qui en avait vu des centaines.
« Ça prendra quelques minutes », annonça-t-il, sortant ses outils avec une précision presque machinale.
Le vieil homme attendit en silence, les mains croisées, le regard perdu quelque part au-delà du magasin.
Après un dernier déclic, le couvercle céda enfin, révélant une pile de lettres jaunies par le temps.
Bernard reconnut, sur l'enveloppe du dessus, une écriture qu'il croyait avoir oubliée depuis des années.
C'était la sienne.
Le vieil homme sourit doucement : « Tu ne te souviens vraiment de rien, n'est-ce pas ? »
Bernard resta sans voix, la boîte tremblant légèrement entre ses propres mains.
Dehors, la nuit était tombée, et le magasin, pour la première fois depuis quarante ans, resta ouvert plus longtemps que prévu.
passages.english:
The shop was closing in ten minutes when the door bell rang one last time.
Bernard looked up without much enthusiasm: another customer, at this hour.
An elderly man walked up to the counter, a small wooden box in his hands.
"I'd like you to open it," he said simply, setting the box down in front of Bernard.
"It's been locked for so long that I've forgotten why."
Bernard examined the lock, tiny and rusted, with the eye of a man who had seen hundreds of them.
"It'll take a few minutes," he announced, taking out his tools with an almost mechanical precision.
The old man waited in silence, hands crossed, his gaze lost somewhere beyond the shop.
After one final click, the lid finally gave way, revealing a stack of letters yellowed with time.
Bernard recognised, on the top envelope, handwriting he thought he had forgotten years ago.
It was his own.
The old man smiled gently: "You really don't remember anything, do you?"
Bernard stood speechless, the box trembling slightly between his own hands.
Outside, night had fallen, and the shop, for the first time in forty years, stayed open longer than planned.
